Because of industrialized agriculture.

Firstly when a machine (or human) is picking the fruit they do not discriminate between ripe and semi-ripe fruit. They pick all because they do not want to return to the same tree (it costs time and money). So you end up with a harvest of mixed quality fruit. This is later sorted by quality but the sorting process is designed to optimize profit, not quality.

Second, slightly green fruit can be stored for longer and last longer on the shelves.

Third, artificial ripening. Most fruit you eat has been artificially ripened with acetylene. It never tastes as good as the real deal.

This is the best answer so far. Also, fruit quality in the business market is rated by looks (Grade A, B etc) and not ever by taste. I believe Californian farmers are only allowed to export Grade A fruit, solely based on colour, size and shape. Green oranges that are perfectly tasty will never see the light of store shelves.

Another more subtle reason are that the fruit cultivars that are easy to grow in a consistent way and therefore easier and more cost effective to grow are not the most delicious. Efficient, low-cost industrial processing is a more important concern for the people selling fruit than taste and the consumers generally don't know any better to demand tastier fruit.

Neoreactionary libertarian capitalist monarchist.

I used to be an anarcho-capitalist, but with the understanding that while anarchy is, IMO, the best form of government, it will almost assuredly fall apart and implode if you are dealing with a group of more than a few dozen people (much like how, IMO, Marxism would). This led me to libertarianism, which - I felt - was the closest thing you could get to anarchy without anarchy's inherent instabilities, while also being a political party in the US that has some traction, and thus a tiny chance of actually going somewhere.

In recent times, however, my views have shifted; I have come to the decision that democracy is, overall, a failure. This belief began with my investigations of alternatives to "first past the post," and has since ended with me deciding that most people - including myself - are simply too ignorant regarding matters of state to make reasonable decisions about who should occupy offices. While I am smart enough to understand politics, there is simply too much there, and I have other things to attend to; I'm sure this goes for the vast majority of other people, where the amount of time spent understanding the issues at hand could have been better spent focusing on their skills and livelihoods. The remainder are idiots, and while I respect their right to vote under a democratic system, I would prefer a system that did not enable them.

I have also found fault with the notion of term limits itself, and the means by which we choose our representatives. Giving the POTUS at most an eight-year window in which to accomplish their goals leads to short-sighted and self-serving behavior, without almost any concern for the future of the state; while that may not have been the case in the past, it feels that way now. In congress and the senate, individuals have served for periods of over double my lifetime: my reaction to this, initially, was that it was obscene, but now I feel that it makes sense, and if we're going to have this be the case, we may as well institutionalize this method, so that they can stop campaigning and worrying about currying favor with business and instead get to the business of governing.

A monarch that actually rules, rather than serves as a figurehead, would obviously be in danger of becoming a tyrant. But I feel that democracy has failed us in that way, as well: in monarchies in the past, tyrants led to revolutions and overthrowing of governments. In democracies, we become convinced that "our guy will win next time," lulling us into a false sense of security that the system is just, when it has shown us over and over again that it is anything but.

This is not to say that the American democracy has not come up with solid institutions. The division of our government into three branches that more-or-less balance each other is a powerful political notion, and one that I would not be willing to sacrifice even in a monarchy system. Ultimately I think that we need to bring back monarchies, but armed with the knowledge we have gained from the democratic experiment, and use the institutions and practices that have actually gotten us the results we want in future alternative governmental systems.
